title: Ketamin improves pain in amputees
summary:
Phantom limb pain (PLP) occurs with an average frequency of 64%. Pre-, peri- and post-operative factors are decisive for the risk and chronification of PLP, while age and gender play a subordinate role. Vascular damage and tumours increase the risk, whereas traumatic amputations are rarely associated with PLP. Other risk factors include preoperative pain, the extent of the amputation, postoperative complaints (such as non-painful sensations) and psychological comorbidities.

In addition to phantom limb pain, residual limb pain (RLP) often occurs, which must be distinguished from wound pain. Both types of pain are influenced by surgery-related lesions of peripheral nerves and central remodelling processes. Varying pathomechanisms of PLP development are reflected in the heterogeneous therapeutic approaches. Mirror therapy in particular supports the hypothesis of central nervous remodelling. Drug treatment approaches, on the other hand, show inconsistent results.

A Germany-wide survey shows major differences in the perioperative prevention of PLP. While almost half of doctors use ketamine perioperatively, there is a lack of standardised practice in accordance with the S3 guideline. The short-term efficacy of ketamine has been proven, but long-term effects remain unresearched. There are concerns regarding side effects at high doses.

The aim of the present study is a longitudinal investigation of the pain therapy established for patients undergoing on-site amputation in order to evaluate its efficacy and safety.

interventions.name: pre- and acute postoperative evaluation (POD 0-5) of pain levels during amputation

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Amputation surgery
In domo ≥3 days
Signed declaration of consent based on the Declaration of Helsinki, if < 18 years by legal guardian
Exclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of dementia, cognitive impairment 
Lack of consent
Insufficient knowledge of German
